traditions.name: Class Plaques of the Inner Quad
traditions.description: Each graduating class buries a time capsule and marks it with a bronze plaque in the walkway around the Inner Quad, starting with 1896 in front of Memorial Church. Walk the arcade and look for a class year.

traditions.name: Hoover Tower Observation Deck
traditions.description: An observation deck 250 feet up gives wide views of campus, and on clear days the San Francisco skyline. The tower also holds a carillon given by the Belgian American Educational Foundation.

traditions.name: Memorial Church Cherubs
traditions.description: Local legend says the stone cherubs carved above the chancel niches and on the pillar capitals were modelled on children living on campus while the church was built. Look up and find them inside the church.

details.airportInfo: SFO is roughly a half-hour drive north of campus. San José's Mineta airport (SJC) is a similar distance to the south.
details.funFact: Stanford's Main Quad was designed by Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge, the successors of Henry Hobson Richardson. They blended his round-arched Romanesque style with a California Mission theme, building in local yellow sandstone under red tile roofs.
details.languageInfo: Students call the campus 'The Farm', after Leland Stanford's horse farm that once stood here, and Memorial Church is simply 'MemChu'.
details.transportationFact: The core of campus around the Main Quad is easy to walk. The free Marguerite shuttle connects the campus with the Palo Alto Caltrain station.

buildings.name: Main Quad
buildings.description: The oldest part of Stanford is a ring of sandstone buildings joined by shaded arcades of round Romanesque arches. It survived two great earthquakes and has looked almost the same from outside since 1906.

buildings.name: Stanford Memorial Church
buildings.description: Jane Stanford built this church in memory of her husband Leland. Romanesque in form and Byzantine in detail, it is inspired by the churches of Venice and Ravenna, and nearly every surface inside is covered in mosaic or carving.

buildings.name: Hoover Tower
buildings.description: Inspired by the tower of the New Cathedral of Salamanca, this 87-metre tower was finished for Stanford's 50th anniversary. It houses Herbert Hoover's library of war, revolution and peace, a 48-bell carillon and an observation deck with views to San Francisco on clear days.

buildings.name: Hanna–Honeycomb House
buildings.description: Frank Lloyd Wright's first work in the Bay Area is laid out on a hexagonal grid, the first non-rectangular plan he ever designed. Built for a Stanford professor, it is now a National Historic Landmark.

buildings.name: Bing Concert Hall
buildings.description: An oval hall with 842 seats arranged in vineyard-style terraces around the stage, so that no seat is more than 75 feet from the conductor. The acoustics are by Yasuhisa Toyota, who also tuned Walt Disney Concert Hall.

traditions.name: The Campanile
traditions.description: Ride the elevator to the observation deck of Sather Tower for views of campus and the Bay. The carillon plays short daily concerts, and on the last day of classes it plays "They're Hanging Danny Deever in the Morning" before going silent for finals.

traditions.name: The 4.0 Ball
traditions.description: Students rub or kiss the stone ball in front of the Campanile for good luck, especially after stepping on a University seal. Give it a touch on your way past.

traditions.name: Athena at Doe Library
traditions.description: Legend says walking under the statue of Athena at the Doe Library entrance gives you wisdom, but walking back out under her takes it away. Students leave by the back doors to keep it.

traditions.name: Hike to the Big C
traditions.description: A walk from near the Foothill parking area leads up to the Big C on the hillside above campus, a hike almost every Cal student makes. Enjoy the view back over campus and the Bay.

details.airportInfo: Oakland's airport is the closest to campus. BART trains link both Oakland and San Francisco International to Downtown Berkeley station, a short walk from Sather Gate.
details.funFact: John Galen Howard shaped the heart of the campus with a Beaux-Arts plan. He designed the Greek Theatre, the Hearst Mining Building, Sather Gate and the Campanile, which is one of the tallest bell-and-clock towers in the world.
details.languageInfo: Locals call the university simply 'Cal', and Sather Tower is known to everyone as 'the Campanile'.
details.transportationFact: Downtown Berkeley BART station sits a few blocks west of the campus. Inside the campus, everything from Sather Gate to the Greek Theatre is within walking distance.

buildings.name: Sather Tower
buildings.description: Known to everyone as the Campanile, this 307-foot clock tower was modelled on St Mark's Campanile in Venice. Its 61-bell carillon can be heard across the city, and its cool, dry interior stores fossils from the La Brea Tar Pits.
buildings.address: Sather Tower, UC Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720
buildings.newUse: Bell tower, observation deck and fossil storage

buildings.name: Doe Memorial Library
buildings.description: Émile Bénard won the design competition for this Neoclassical library, which faces Memorial Glade. Its grand reading rooms sit above the underground Gardner Main Stacks.
buildings.address: Doe Library, UC Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720

buildings.name: Hearst Memorial Mining Building
buildings.description: The first building John Galen Howard designed for the campus, created with help from Julia Morgan as a memorial to the miner George Hearst. A 1998–2003 renovation slid a seismic platform under the historic building.
buildings.address: Hearst Memorial Mining Building, UC Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720

buildings.name: Hearst Greek Theatre
buildings.description: Modelled directly on the ancient theatre of Epidaurus, this 8,500-seat amphitheatre opened in 1903 with a student production of Aristophanes' The Birds. It still hosts concerts and graduation ceremonies.

buildings.name: Sather Gate
buildings.description: This gate between Sproul Plaza and the bridge over Strawberry Creek has been the classic way into the centre of campus since 1910. Jane Sather gave it in memory of her husband Peder.
buildings.address: Sather Gate, UC Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720

buildings.name: Hearst Gymnasium for Women
buildings.description: Bernard Maybeck and Julia Morgan designed this symmetrical gymnasium as William Randolph Hearst's memorial to his mother Phoebe. It once offered women students three outdoor swimming pools.

traditions.name: Rub the Bruin Bear's Paw
traditions.description: Students rub the paw of the Bruin Bear statue in Bruin Plaza for good luck during finals week. Visitors stop for a photo and a paw rub.

traditions.name: Skip the Sixth Step
traditions.description: Legend says anyone who steps on the sixth step of Janss Steps will have bad luck and graduate a quarter late. Many students hop over it on the way up.

traditions.name: Inverted Fountain
traditions.description: New students are "Bruintized" at this 1968 fountain, whose water drops into a well instead of spraying up. Tradition says they then avoid touching the water until graduation, so visitors look but do not touch.

details.airportInfo: LAX is the closest major airport to Westwood, usually a short drive north along the San Diego Freeway, depending on traffic.
details.funFact: Royce Hall and Powell Library, two of the four original buildings on the Westwood campus, face each other across the main quad. Both are brick Romanesque Revival buildings modelled on the Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio in Milan.
details.languageInfo: Students are Bruins, and the twin towers of Royce Hall are the image of UCLA you will see on almost every brochure.
details.transportationFact: The central campus is compact enough to explore on foot. Many Los Angeles Metro bus lines stop around the edges of the Westwood campus.

buildings.name: Royce Hall
buildings.description: The twin-towered brick front of Royce Hall, inspired by Milan's Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio, is the best-known landmark at UCLA. Its 1,800-seat auditorium was built for lectures but grew into a major concert hall.
buildings.newUse: Concert hall and performing arts venue

buildings.name: Powell Library
buildings.description: Facing Royce Hall across the quad, Powell Library is also modelled on Sant'Ambrogio. Its central tower is topped by an octagonal dome, and Renaissance printers' marks decorate the ceiling of the main reading room.
buildings.address: Powell Library, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA 90095

buildings.name: Charles E. Young Research Library
buildings.description: A Mid-Century Modern library of concrete frame and dark glass at the north edge of campus, designed by A. Quincy Jones and Frederick Earl Emmons. It is one of the largest libraries at UCLA.
buildings.architect: A. Quincy Jones and Frederick Earl Emmons
buildings.address: Charles E. Young Research Library, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA 90095

buildings.name: Franklin D. Murphy Sculpture Garden
buildings.description: Landscape architect Ralph Cornell laid out this five-acre garden in 1967. More than 70 sculptures by artists like Henry Moore, Rodin, Calder and Noguchi stand among its lawns and trees.
buildings.address: Franklin D. Murphy Sculpture Garden, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA 90095

traditions.name: Cherry Blossoms in the Quad
traditions.description: Visiting the Yoshino cherry trees in the Quad when they bloom each spring is a must-do UW tradition. Expect crowds of students and visitors taking photos at peak bloom.

traditions.name: Rainier Vista
traditions.description: The view down Rainier Vista past Drumheller Fountain is protected so nothing can block Mount Rainier from Red Square. On a clear day, stand at the top for the best view on campus.

traditions.name: Sylvan Grove Columns
traditions.description: Four cedar columns from the UW's first downtown building stand in Sylvan Grove and represent loyalty, industry, faith and efficiency. New students touch one when they arrive and again at graduation; visitors can see them in the grove.

traditions.name: The Wave at Husky Stadium
traditions.description: UW says the famous stadium wave began at Husky Stadium during a 1981 football game. Join in when it rolls around the stands on game day.

details.airportInfo: Sea-Tac sits south of Seattle. Link light rail runs from the airport straight to University of Washington station, next to Husky Stadium.
details.funFact: Architect Carl Gould laid out the Liberal Arts Quadrangle in 1915, and its Collegiate Gothic halls are lined with thirty Yoshino cherry trees that bloom between mid-March and early April.
details.languageInfo: The university is 'U-Dub' to almost everyone, and the red-brick Central Plaza is always called Red Square.
details.transportationFact: Link light rail stops at University of Washington station by Husky Stadium. From there the central campus, from Red Square to the Quad, is an easy walk.

buildings.name: Suzzallo Library
buildings.description: The Collegiate Gothic façade of Suzzallo dominates Red Square, and its Graduate Reading Room is one of the most photographed rooms in Seattle. The architects planned a 300-foot bell tower that was never built.
buildings.architect: Charles H. Bebb and Carl F. Gould
buildings.address: Suzzallo Library, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195

buildings.name: Denny Hall
buildings.description: Built of brick and sandstone in 1894–95, Denny Hall is the oldest building on the current campus. It is named after Seattle pioneer Arthur A. Denny.
buildings.address: Denny Hall, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195

buildings.name: University of Washington Quad
buildings.description: The Liberal Arts Quadrangle is UW's trademark: brick Gothic halls framing a lawn lined with thirty Yoshino cherry trees. Carl Gould drew its layout in 1915, though it was not finished until 1950.
buildings.address: Liberal Arts Quadrangle, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195

buildings.name: Gerberding Hall
buildings.description: The first major building raised on campus after World War II, this Collegiate Gothic hall on Red Square was built for the university's administrative offices in 1949.
buildings.architect: Victor N. Jones and John T. Jacobsen

buildings.name: Odegaard Undergraduate Library
buildings.description: A Brutalist library at the corner of Red Square, built together with the parking garage beneath the plaza. Its 2013 interior renovation won an AIA Institute Honor Award.
buildings.address: Odegaard Undergraduate Library, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195

buildings.name: Henry Art Gallery
buildings.description: Founded in 1927 as the first public art museum in Washington state, the Henry sits on the west edge of campus. Bebb and Gould designed the original building, and Gwathmey Siegel expanded it in 1997.
buildings.architect: Bebb and Gould; Gwathmey Siegel & Associates (1997 expansion)

traditions.name: Chimes of the Roddick Gates
traditions.description: The Roddick Gates, McGill's formal entrance on Sherbrooke Street, carry four clocks whose bells strike the Westminster Quarters. Walk through the gates onto campus and listen for the chimes.

traditions.name: James McGill's Tomb
traditions.description: The remains of founder James McGill rest in a monument in front of the Arts Building, moved there from a Montreal cemetery and consecrated in 1875. Visitors can stop by the founder's tomb on the lower campus.

traditions.name: Photo at the Three Bares
traditions.description: The Three Bares fountain, unveiled at Spring Convocation in 1931 in a tree-lined dell near the Redpath Museum, appears in countless convocation photographs. Visitors can take their own photo at this well-known campus landmark.

details.airportInfo: Trudeau airport is in Dorval, west of downtown. The 747 express bus runs from the airport into the city centre, a short walk from the Roddick Gates.
details.funFact: McGill's oldest building, the Arts Building, was begun in 1839 to a Classical Revival design by John Ostell. Around it stand a Victorian Greek Revival museum, a Richardsonian Romanesque library hall and a Brutalist library from the 1960s.
details.languageInfo: McGill is an English-language university in French-speaking Montreal, so you will hear both languages all over campus and on the streets around it.
details.transportationFact: The downtown campus climbs the slope of Mount Royal from Sherbrooke Street. McGill metro station on the Green Line is a few blocks south of the main gates.

buildings.name: Arts Building
buildings.description: The oldest building on campus, begun in 1839, sits at the top of the main avenue with its Classical Revival portico. Wings were added in 1861 and 1925, and Moyse Hall theatre fills the north wing.

buildings.name: Redpath Museum
buildings.description: Sugar baron Peter Redpath gave McGill the oldest building in Canada built specifically as a museum. Its own university calls it an unusual and late example of the Greek Revival in North America.
buildings.architect: A. C. Hutchison and A. D. Steele

buildings.name: Redpath Hall
buildings.description: Once the reading room of McGill's first library building, this Richardsonian Romanesque hall is now a concert venue run by the Schulich School of Music. It has a French Classical pipe organ by Hellmuth Wolff.

buildings.name: Macdonald-Harrington Building
buildings.description: Built in 1896–97 as the chemistry building, a gift of tobacco magnate Sir William Macdonald. Today it houses all of McGill's architecture studios, so future architects learn inside a Renaissance Revival landmark.
buildings.newUse: School of Architecture and School of Urban Planning

buildings.name: McLennan Library Building
buildings.description: A seven-storey reinforced concrete library built in 1967–69 next to the old Redpath Library. Together they form McGill's largest library, the Humanities and Social Sciences Library.

traditions.name: Reznikoff's Gargoyles
traditions.description: University College's best-known ghost story says stonemason Ivan Reznikoff was killed by a rival while the building was going up in the 1850s. Visitors can look for the two gargoyles said to show the rivals' faces near UC's southwest corner, where a door is said to bear an axe mark.

traditions.name: The Weeping Stone Face
traditions.description: Campus ghost lore includes a carved stone face at Hart House that is said to have wept water from one eye. Visitors to Hart House can look for the face among its Gothic stonework.

traditions.name: Soldiers' Tower Carillon
traditions.description: The 51 bells of the Soldiers' Tower carillon honour university members who died in the World Wars, and they ring out for free public recitals and around convocation. Listen from the Hart House Circle lawn or the University College quadrangle.

details.airportInfo: Pearson is northwest of downtown. The UP Express train runs from the airport to Union Station, where the subway goes north to the campus.
details.funFact: The St. George campus spans the eras: University College's Romanesque Revival main building is a National Historic Site, Hart House and Soldiers' Tower are Gothic, and Robarts Library is a Brutalist giant nicknamed 'Fort Book'.
details.languageInfo: Everyone calls the university 'U of T', and its students belong to colleges such as University College, Trinity and Victoria.
details.transportationFact: The campus sits in downtown Toronto beside Queen's Park. Queen's Park, Museum and St. George subway stations all lie along its edges.

buildings.name: University College
buildings.description: Frederick William Cumberland designed University College's main building, completed in 1859. The Romanesque Revival landmark on King's College Circle is a National Historic Site of Canada.

buildings.name: Hart House
buildings.description: One of the earliest student centres in North America, financed by Vincent Massey and named for his grandfather Hart Massey. The Collegiate Gothic complex wraps around a quadrangle and has hosted student debates since it opened.

buildings.name: Soldiers' Tower
buildings.description: This 43.6-metre Gothic Revival bell tower, attached to Hart House, honours university members who served in the World Wars. It holds a carillon of 51 bells.
buildings.architect: Henry Sproatt and Ernest Ross Rolph

buildings.name: Convocation Hall
buildings.description: A domed rotunda whose radial auditorium has been compared to the Sorbonne's grand amphitheatre and Oxford's Sheldonian Theatre. Every convocation ceremony from all three campuses is held here.

buildings.name: Robarts Library
buildings.description: A Brutalist tower on a triangular footprint, with triangles repeated throughout. Its imposing look earned it the nicknames 'Fort Book' and 'the Peacock'.
buildings.architect: Mathers & Haldenby; Warner, Burns, Toan & Lunde

traditions.name: The Great Trek Cairn
traditions.description: This stone cairn on Main Mall marks the 1922 Great Trek, when students marched to Point Grey to push the government to finish the campus, and it was built from stones gathered on site. A ceremony is held there each September during Homecoming, and visitors can read its inscription any time.

traditions.name: The Painted Engineering Cairn
traditions.description: Engineering students look after a concrete monument on Main Mall that is repainted for causes, anniversaries and campus events. Visitors can stop by to see its latest paint job.

traditions.name: Ladner Clock Tower Chimes
traditions.description: The Ladner Clock Tower in front of the Main Library chimes on the hour, and its carillon plays short sets during the day and on special occasions such as convocation. Visitors can listen from the Library Garden.

details.airportInfo: YVR is on Sea Island in Richmond, south of the campus. The Canada Line takes you into Vancouver, where buses continue west to the UBC Exchange.
details.funFact: UBC's Brock Commons Tallwood House was the tallest mass timber building in the world when it opened in 2017, and Arthur Erickson's Museum of Anthropology recreates the post-and-beam houses of Northwest Coast First Nations in concrete.
details.languageInfo: The campus sits on Point Grey, and it is not officially part of the City of Vancouver, even though everyone thinks of it as Vancouver.
details.transportationFact: Frequent buses run from downtown Vancouver and the Canada Line to the UBC Exchange in the centre of campus. From there, Main Mall leads on foot to most of the buildings.

buildings.name: Museum of Anthropology
buildings.description: Arthur Erickson's concrete museum takes its form from the post-and-beam houses of Northwest Coast First Nations. Bill Reid's sculpture The Raven and the First Men sits on a repurposed wartime gun battery.
buildings.newUse: Museum of world arts and cultures

buildings.wiki: Chan Centre for the Performing Arts
buildings.name: Chan Centre for the Performing Arts
buildings.description: A concert hall set among evergreens and rhododendrons, with a 37-tonne acoustic canopy of steel and cork hanging over the stage. Cornelia Oberlander designed its landscape.
buildings.address: Chan Centre, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC

buildings.name: Brock Commons Tallwood House
buildings.description: An 18-storey student residence that was the tallest mass timber structure in the world when it opened. It stands 53 metres tall.

buildings.name: C. K. Choi Building
buildings.description: A pioneer of green design, built on an old parking lot with about half of its materials recycled or reused, and with natural ventilation. Its architecture uses Asian motifs for the Institute of Asian Research inside.

buildings.name: Nitobe Memorial Garden
buildings.description: A traditional Japanese garden honouring the diplomat Nitobe Inazō, who hoped to be a bridge across the Pacific. Kannosuke Mori of Chiba University designed it, and it opened in June 1960.

traditions.name: Day of the Dead Megaofrenda
traditions.description: Each year around Day of the Dead, UNAM schools and offices build a giant collective offering of altars, long held at Las Islas, the central lawn of Ciudad Universitaria. Visitors can walk among the altars for free in early November.

traditions.name: Central Library Mosaic
traditions.description: Juan O'Gorman's stone mosaic covers all four sides of the Central Library, each side showing a different era of Mexican history. Walk around the building to see every side and take a photo of this campus icon.

traditions.name: Rectory Tower Murals
traditions.description: The Rectory Tower carries three murals by David Alfaro Siqueiros and, at the top, the university coat of arms with the motto 'Por mi raza hablará el espíritu'. Visitors can view the murals and the shield from the esplanade.

traditions.name: Diego Rivera Relief at the Olympic Stadium
traditions.description: The main entrance of the Estadio Olímpico Universitario features a relief by Diego Rivera made of naturally coloured stones, and the stadium still has its 1968 Olympic cauldron. Visitors can see the relief from outside the stadium.

details.airportInfo: Benito Juárez International is on the east side of Mexico City. The campus is in Coyoacán in the south, so plan on a long taxi or Metro ride across the city.
details.funFact: Ciudad Universitaria was built in the 1950s on a lava bed left by the Xitle volcano around 100 AD. UNESCO named its central campus a World Heritage Site in 2007 for the way it joins modern architecture with murals by Mexican artists.
details.languageInfo: Classes and campus life are in Spanish. The main campus is simply 'C.U.' (say-oo) to students.
details.transportationFact: The university runs its own free Pumabús routes around the huge campus. Universidad and Copilco Metro stations on Line 3 serve the campus.

buildings.name: Ciudad Universitaria
buildings.description: Mario Pani and Enrique del Moral planned this vast modern campus, completed in 1954 on the old lava fields of El Pedregal. Its central campus is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, known for blending modern buildings with murals by Siqueiros, Chávez Morado and Eppens.
buildings.architect: Mario Pani and Enrique del Moral
buildings.address: Av. Universidad 3000, Ciudad Universitaria, Coyoacán, Mexico City

buildings.name: Central Library
buildings.description: UNAM's most famous building is wrapped on all four sides in Juan O'Gorman's mural Historical Representation of Culture, made from natural coloured stones he collected all over Mexico. Its ten windowless upper floors were built to store books.
buildings.architect: Juan O'Gorman, Gustavo Saavedra and Juan Martínez de Velasco

buildings.name: Estadio Olímpico Universitario
buildings.description: The main stadium of the 1968 Summer Olympics, opened in 1952 as Mexico's largest. Diego Rivera's relief of coloured stones over the main entrance shows the university shield, a family and a feathered serpent.
buildings.architect: Augusto Pérez Palacios, Jorge Bravo and Raúl Salinas
buildings.address: Av. Insurgentes Sur s/n, Ciudad Universitaria, Coyoacán, Mexico City

buildings.name: Museo Universitario Arte Contemporáneo
buildings.description: Teodoro González de León designed this contemporary art museum with a minimalist, sloping glass façade that contrasts with the 1970s University Cultural Center around it. It opened in 2008.
buildings.address: Av. de los Insurgentes Sur 3000, Coyoacán, Mexico City

traditions.name: The Fleming Cannon
traditions.description: A Franco-Prussian War-era cannon rests on its wheels in front of Fleming House and is fired only for big moments like commencement. MIT students once hauled it across the country as a prank. Stop by to see it.

traditions.name: The Turtle Pond
traditions.description: Dozens of turtles, mostly red-eared sliders, live in the pond in Throop Memorial Garden, where Caltech's first building once stood. Look for them sunning on the rocks, but don't feed them.

traditions.name: Watson Lectures
traditions.description: For about a century Caltech scientists have explained their work in free public talks, today called the Watson Lectures and held at Beckman Auditorium. Catch one in person or online.

traditions.name: Halloween Pumpkin Drop
traditions.description: Every Halloween, students drop pumpkins frozen in liquid nitrogen from the top of Caltech Hall, the former Millikan Library, while a crowd watches for a spark. The name nods to Millikan's famous oil-drop experiment.

traditions.name: Tournament Park
traditions.description: The athletic field at Tournament Park, on the south side of campus, hosted the first Rose Bowl games. Walk past the track to see where the famous game began.

details.nickname: The truth shall make you free
details.airportInfo: Hollywood Burbank Airport is the closest airport to Caltech. Los Angeles International (LAX) has many more flights but is a longer drive across the city.
details.funFact: NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory grew out of rocket research at Caltech's Guggenheim lab in the 1930s, and Caltech still manages JPL today.
details.languageInfo: Write it 'Caltech', one word: the institute considers spellings like 'Cal Tech' incorrect. The school color is orange, and the teams are the Beavers.
details.transportationFact: The compact campus is easy to walk. Metro A Line light rail stops at Lake and Allen stations, about a mile north of campus.

buildings.name: The Athenaeum
buildings.description: Gordon Kaufmann designed this Mediterranean Revival faculty club, which opened in 1930 with gardens by Florence Yoch and Lucile Council. Albert Einstein stayed here during his winter visits to Caltech.
buildings.address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125

buildings.name: Beckman Institute
buildings.description: Albert C. Martin & Associates designed this Spanish-style research building around a courtyard and reflecting pool. Funded by Arnold and Mabel Beckman and dedicated in 1989, it hosts chemistry and biology research and the Caltech Science Museum.
buildings.address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125

buildings.name: Guggenheim Aeronautical Laboratory
buildings.description: Opened in 1929 with money from the Daniel Guggenheim Fund, this lab became the first university rocket research center under Theodore von Kármán, work that led to the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Carvings over its doors show the Douglas World Cruisers that first flew around the world.
buildings.architect: Mayers, Murray & Phillip (Goodhue Associates); Clarence S. Stein
buildings.address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125

buildings.wiki: Campus of the California Institute of Technology
buildings.name: Beckman Auditorium
buildings.description: Edward Durell Stone designed this round white concert hall, a gift of Arnold and Mabel Beckman that opened with a gala concert in 1964. Its 1,136 seats host Caltech's public lectures, shows and films.
buildings.address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125

buildings.wiki: Campus of the California Institute of Technology
buildings.name: Caltech Hall
buildings.description: The nine-story former Millikan Library is the tallest building on campus; its donor argued a tower would save green space on a low-rise campus. Completed in 1967, it was renamed Caltech Hall in 2021 and now holds offices and study space.
buildings.address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125

buildings.wiki: Campus of the California Institute of Technology
buildings.name: Dabney Hall
buildings.description: Planned by Bertram Goodhue's office and opened in 1928, Dabney Hall is one of the oldest buildings on campus. It still houses the humanities, with Dabney Lounge and the Humanities Library inside.
buildings.architect: Mayers, Murray & Phillip (Goodhue Associates); Clarence S. Stein
buildings.address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125

buildings.wiki: Campus of the California Institute of Technology
buildings.name: Parsons-Gates Hall of Administration
buildings.description: Built in 1917 as the first unit of the Gates chemistry labs, this is the oldest building still standing on campus. Damaged in the 1971 San Fernando earthquake, it was rebuilt in 1983 for the offices of the president and provost.
buildings.architect: Elmer Grey; Bertram Goodhue (1917); Bobrow/Thomas & Associates (1983 rebuild)
buildings.address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125

buildings.wiki: Campus of the California Institute of Technology
buildings.name: Norman Bridge Laboratory of Physics
buildings.description: Bertram Goodhue designed this physics lab, first occupied in 1922 and the oldest academic building on campus. Robert Millikan had his laboratories here, and its second floor holds the Feynman Lecture Hall.
buildings.address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125

buildings.wiki: Campus of the California Institute of Technology
buildings.name: Kerckhoff Laboratories of the Biological Sciences
buildings.description: Opened in 1928, Kerckhoff is home to Caltech biology. Ed Lewis worked here on fruit fly genetics, research that won the 1995 Nobel Prize, and it keeps one of the few fruit fly collections in the US.
buildings.architect: Mayers, Murray & Phillip (Goodhue Associates); Clarence S. Stein
buildings.address: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125

buildings.wiki: Campus of the California Institute of Technology
buildings.name: Cahill Center for Astronomy and Astrophysics
buildings.description: Thom Mayne's firm Morphosis designed this astronomy center, which opened in 2009 as the first building on campus to earn LEED Gold. Its street number, 1216, is the wavelength of ultraviolet light given off by hydrogen.
